name: Eyelash implants

lead: Eyelash implants, also called eyelash transplantation, place hair into the eyelid margin so it grows as lashes. The goal is permanently fuller, more defined eyes without glued-on extensions.

Hair is set into the lid edge so it grows there as lashes. The sources reviewed describe the history of the idea, such as an 1882 report of hair sewn into the eyelids and an 1899 newspaper account, and contain no modern outcome studies.

paras: It is a surgical procedure done on the eyelid, unlike extensions or false lashes that are applied to or alongside existing lashes. People weighing it compare it with those removable options.
It is surgery on the eyelid, and historical accounts describe the early method as painful. No modern safety or outcome studies were found.

angle.text: People seeking permanently fuller lashes consider eyelash transplantation, which places hair into the eyelid margin so it grows as lashes. It differs from extensions and false lashes, and the sources reviewed give history only.

lead: Eyelash implants, also called eyelash transplantation, are surgical procedures in which hair follicles are placed along the eyelid margin to create, thicken or lengthen lashes. People seek them for a permanent fuller, darker lash line that frames the eyes without daily mascara, glued-on extensions or serums. They differ from temporary eyelash extensions or false lashes, which are applied to or alongside existing lashes.

The procedure is performed under local anaesthesia, often with mild sedation, with donor hair usually taken from the nape or the scalp behind the ears, though eyebrow or leg hair has also been used [1][2]. The International Society of Hair Restoration Surgery describes candidates as people who lost lashes through trauma, burns, scarring, disease, cancer treatment or trichotillomania, as well as people with sparse lashes who want a cosmetic enhancement [1].

Ophthalmic plastic surgeons have raised concerns about cosmetic use. A 2007 EyeWorld report quoted Emory oculoplastic surgeon Anna Murchison saying cosmetic augmentation exposes the patient to unnecessary risks, and listed complications such as trichiasis, corneal abrasion and scarring [3]. Clinical literature is limited to case reports and a systematic review of eyebrow and eyelash transplantation [2][4].

paras: The surgeon makes tiny punctures in the lid margin and places individual hair grafts, spacing them to avoid trichiasis, where lashes grow inward. A session takes one to three hours and desired density usually takes one to three sessions [1]. Itching is common for a day or more, and scratching can dislodge grafts, so protective goggles are often worn during sleep; full recovery is described as taking about 7 to 14 days [1]. Afterwards the transplanted hairs are curled and trimmed regularly because scalp hair keeps growing [1].
A 2018 systematic review of eyebrow and eyelash transplantation found follicular unit techniques were the most common, with composite grafts and flaps also used [2][4].

The International Society of Hair Restoration Surgery lists eyelid infection, bruising and swelling, graft displacement or failed growth, ingrown hairs, ectropion, entropion and poor graft placement or quality [1]. EyeWorld's 2007 report adds corneal abrasion and scarring, a foreign-body sensation and, in extreme cases, a threat to vision, and notes lashes that need ongoing trimming and may not look natural [3]. The society says results can be a significant improvement but cannot be completely natural [1].

Carl Heinrich Dzondi of Halle made the earliest documented attempt to transplant individual eyelashes in 1817 to 1818 [2]. Techniques using grafts of eyebrow margin (1838), a trephine and syringe (1914) and rotated lid-margin flaps (1919) followed, and Japanese dermatologists' work on small hair grafts fed the modern scalp-hair method in the late twentieth century [2]. A 2015 report described the first eyelash transplant using leg hair, and a 2016 series treated vitiligo-related lash whitening with follicular unit transplantation [2].

Separately, press accounts from 1882 and 1899 describe hair being sewn into eyelids to make false lashes [5]. Wikipedia recounts that false eyelashes were patented in the UK by Karl Nessler (filed 1902) and in the US by Anna Taylor (1911), and that in 1916 human-hair lashes fixed with spirit gum were used on actress Seena Owen in the film Intolerance [5]. Temporary lashes became popular in the early 1930s [5].

Prescription bimatoprost, sold for lashes as Latisse, is applied to the lash base to make small or underdeveloped lashes more prominent [6][7]. A registered study examined patient satisfaction with combined botulinum toxin, hyaluronic acid filler and Latisse for facial lines [8].
A 2018 systematic review of eyebrow and eyelash hair transplantation exists, covering the published case literature [4]. No controlled trials of cosmetic eyelash implants were found.
